extracted.intended_audience: general readers, aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy researchers and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for creating, performing, and understanding live stand-up comedy, including genres, routine construction, delivery, audience interaction, and professional roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of stand-up comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up comedy is an art form that involves a stand-up comic and an audience; a comic delivers humorous and satirical monologues, sometimes incorporating physical acts (act outs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances are typically composed of tightly crafted sets or acts, and often include varying degrees of live crowd interaction (crowdwork).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical components and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up consists of one-liners, stories, observations, or shticks that can employ props, music, impressions, dialects, magic tricks, or ventriloquism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians may combine these tools as part of their set to enhance variety and entertainment value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venues and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances can take place in comedy clubs, comedy festivals, bars, nightclubs, colleges, casino showrooms, or theaters; during the pandemic also on video conferencing, social media, rooftops and open-air locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of venue affects show format, audience expectations, and appropriate material/length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres and styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up has multiple genres and styles such as alternative (alt-) comedy, anecdotal (storytelling), character, deadpan (dry humour), impressionist, insult, musical, observational, satire, topical, wordplay, self-deprecating, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each genre has its own conventions and delivery expectations (e.g., wordplay favors one-liners; anecdotal favors extended storytelling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine structure (bits and closer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines are constructed from jokes and interconnected 'bits' forming an interwoven narrative that leads to the 'closer', the final joke tying themes together for a satisfying conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material so bits build toward and reinforce the closer; many comics design sets with thematic cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure (premise, set-up, punchline, tags)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes are the juxtaposition of two incongruous things made up of the premise, set-up, and punchline, often adding a twist, topper, or tagline for extra laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear premises and setups to prepare the audience; tags/topper can intensify or extend the laugh after the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery elements (timing, intonation, attitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery relies on intonation, inflection, attitude, and timing as well as stylistic devices such as the rule of three, idioms, archetypes, or wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master comic timing (including strategic pauses/beat) and vocal/physical delivery to maximize comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraprosdokian and other surprising structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraprosdokian is a popular structure: a surprising punchline that changes the context or meaning of the setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such structures to subvert expectations; they are a recognized mechanism for generating surprise laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jester's privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians can invoke the 'jester's privilege', the right to discuss and mock anything freely without being punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concept is used to frame risky or transgressive material, but does not insulate performers from audience reaction or social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical consideration: punching up vs punching down
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts of 'punching up' and 'punching down' describe who should be the butt of the joke; the assumption is comedy should 'punch up' at the rich and powerful and avoid 'punching down' at marginalized people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians and commentators debate these norms; awareness of social-political identity and power dynamics informs audience reception and professional reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and joke theft norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation and plagiarism (joke theft) are considered 'social crimes' by most stand-ups; accusations can lead to lawsuits but are legally hard to win due to the idea–expression distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid appropriating material; be mindful of parallel thinking and cryptomnesia claims. Reputation among peers is a primary enforcement mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience as co-constructor and arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences are both 'co-constructors' of the situation and 'co-responsible' for it; an unspoken contract allows exploration of unexpected or controversial subjects. The audience's laughter delegates whether a joke worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful comics read and react to audience signals in real time and use those reactions to shape the performance; if the audience is not laughing, the joke is not working.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd work / live interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Live crowd interaction (crowdwork) involves talking directly with audience members through prewritten bits, improvisation, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowdwork requires quick thinking and sensitivity to audience dynamics; can enhance intimacy but risks escalation or heckling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance roles and show order
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows typically have a host/emcee (warms up audience), opener, feature, and headliner. Host may act as opener in small shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headliner generally performs roughly an hour of original material; feature 25–30 minutes; opener ~10 minutes; emcee supplies transition jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open mic and bringer show dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Open mics are used to work on material or get noticed; open mics may be booked or walk-ins. Bringer shows require performers to bring a specified number of paying guests to receive stage time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open mics are for testing/working out material; be aware some open-mic events function as bringer shows with audience requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: TV specials and album runtimes
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'half-hour special' is typically between 20 and 35 minutes runtime excluding commercial breaks; an 'hour-long special' typically between 40 and 65 minutes excluding commercial breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specials may be recorded on tour or at a show performed specifically for recording; runtime expectations inform material pacing and set composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tight five and audition-ready material
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'tight five' is a five-minute routine that is well-rehearsed and consists of a comedian's best material that reliably gets laughs; used for auditions and as a stepping stone to paid spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft and memorize a reliable tight five to showcase your strengths in high-stakes auditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work out / polishing process
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out refers to the process in which brand new jokes are introduced and polished over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly test, revise, and refine material through performances; expect jokes to change with audience feedback and repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm up and reading the room
rubrics_metrics.description: Warm up means to warm a 'cold' audience during an opening act; reading the room enables performers to interpret audience signs and adapt material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use warm-up strategies and adapt pacing/edits to audience receptivity; misreading a room can lead to bombing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombing and other failure/success terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombing or dying means failing to get laughs; terms like killing, crushing, destroying mean doing very well. Anti-patterns include 'chewing the scenery' (being overly theatrical) and 'mugging' (pulling silly faces for cheap laughs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and avoid hacky behavior (clichéd or unskilled comic) and mugging; focus on authentic delivery and material craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clapter and applause vs laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Clapter is when the audience cheers or applauds an opinion they agree with but which is not funny enough to laugh at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between applause for sentiment and genuine comedic laughter; material that generates clapter may be rhetorically effective but not necessarily comedic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of live vs canned laughter in recorded comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Canned laughter in television reveals the importance of a live audience; shows often seem 'dry' without it, and many specials are filmed in front of a live audience for that reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recording, consider how audience reactions (live or artificial) shape perceived funniness and timing.
